title: Herod's Temple
hookLine: a hard king rebuilds the Temple, and one of its great outer walls still stands

lines: NOT THE TEMPLE, BUT ITS WALL.
cards: Folded slips of paper, pushed into the cracks between huge pale stones. Small green plants growing out of the joints.
Some press their foreheads to the stone; some read psalms; some just lay a hand flat on the wall and stay. This is the Western Wall in Jerusalem, in Hebrew the Kotel. It isn't the Temple itself.
It's part of the great outer wall that held up the platform the Temple once stood on. Why pray at a retaining wall? Go back to the man who built it: Herod.

teach.h: A HARD KING REBUILDS THE TEMPLE.
teach.b: Herod was a king of Judea who ruled with Rome's backing. The Jewish historian Josephus tells his story, and it isn't gentle: Josephus records a suspicious, violent king who had members of his own family put to death.
And he set out to rebuild the Second Temple, the house that had stood since the return from Babylon.
Josephus describes the hill enlarged, enormous walls raised to hold up a wide, level court, and a sanctuary so covered in gold and white stone that from far off it looked like a snowy mountain.
The rabbis tell a harder story about how it began. In tractate Bava Batra, Herod has killed the sages. One survives, Bava ben Buta, whom Herod has blinded.
Herod, in disguise, tries to trick him into cursing the king. He won't.

teach.h: A BLINDED SAGE SAYS: TEND THE LIGHT.
teach.b: Herod asks how he could make amends, and the sage answers, in paraphrase: you darkened the light of the world, so go and tend the light of the world. Rebuild the Temple.
The same page keeps a saying, in paraphrase: whoever has not seen Herod's building has never seen a beautiful building. The rabbis keep the cruelty and the beauty, and smooth over neither.
The sanctuary would not last, but part of the western retaining wall did.
One midrash reads a line from the Song of Songs, "behold, he standeth behind our wall", and says God's presence never leaves the Western Wall.
The Hebrew word for wall in that verse is the same word people use for the Kotel.

how: Jews pray at the Western Wall in Jerusalem, and visitors leave folded written prayers in the cracks between its stones.

games.q: you're Bava ben Buta. the king who blinded you asks how he can make amends. what do you say?
o: curse him and refuse to answer.
tell him to rebuild the Temple.
tell him to leave Jerusalem forever.
games.why: in the Talmud's story, the sage won't curse the king. he tells him to tend the light of the world by rebuilding the Temple, and Herod does.

practice: Hold the scene in your mind, or find a picture of the Western Wall, and pick one stone to stay with; someone cut it for Herod, and many hands have touched it since.
Then think of one thing in your life that outlasted something larger, like a recipe that outlived a kitchen. If you pray, you can say a psalm you know, the way people do at the wall.

wordCard.voice: Herod's Temple. Rebuilt by a hard king, praised even by the rabbis who remembered his cruelty, and part of its western wall still stands.

orig.note: Hebrew: wall, the everyday name for the Western Wall in Jerusalem.
